caption: Figure 1: Our reparametrization. We only train A and B .
description:
This figure is a diagram illustrating the LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) method for large language models. It shows the process of adapting a pretrained model by training only two matrices, A and B, while keeping the original weights W fixed. The input x is processed through the pretrained weights W, and then combined with the product of matrices A and B. The matrices A and B are initialized with values from a normal distribution N(0,σ^2). The figure highlights that only A and B are trained during the adaptation process.

caption: Figure 2: GPT-3 175B validation accuracy vs. number of trainable parameters of several adaptation methods on WikiSQL and MNLI-matched. LoRA exhibits better scalability and task performance. See Section F.2 for more details on the plotted data points.
description:
This figure is a line graph comparing the validation accuracy of various adaptation methods for large language models on two datasets: WikiSQL and MultiNLI-matched. The x-axis represents the log10 number of trainable parameters, ranging from 6 to 11. The y-axis shows validation accuracy. The highest accuracy is achieved by LoRA on the MultiNLI-matched dataset, peaking at around 0.92. The lowest accuracy is observed for PrefixLayer on WikiSQL, around 0.55. Other methods include Fine-Tune, PrefixEmbed, Adapter(H), and LoRA.

caption: Figure 8: Normalized subspace similarity between the singular directions of W q and those of ∆ W q with varying r and a random baseline. ∆ W q amplifies directions that are important but not emphasized in W . ∆ W with a larger r tends to pick up more directions that are already emphasized in W .
description:
This figure displays four heatmaps representing the normalized subspace similarity between the singular directions of \( W_q \) and those of \( \Delta W_q \) with varying rank \( r \) and a random baseline. The heatmaps show the similarity scores ranging from -0.200 to 0.100. The first heatmap corresponds to \( \phi(W_q, A_r=4, i, j) \), the second to \( \phi(W_q, A_r=8, i, j) \), the third to \( \phi(W_q, A_r=64, i, j) \), and the fourth to \( \phi(W_q, A_{rand}, i, j) \). The heatmaps show that as \( r \) increases, the similarity scores become more pronounced, indicating that \( \Delta W_q \) amplifies important directions in \( W_q \).
